title: Test Nodics Changes
readerIntent: Select proportional tests that prove a Nodics change across layers, authorities, and deployment topologies.
priorKnowledge: Understand the capability owner, public contracts, configuration, security, and runtime topology.
owner: Owning module tests plus repository-wide Nodics governance and regression suites
summary: Nodics validation proves successful behavior and rejected behavior, boundaries, contracts, integrations, resilience, security, performance, topology, generated artifacts, and regressions.

sections.heading: Test design from the contract
items: Begin with the owning schema, service, route, lifecycle, security, provider, and operational contracts. Map each promise and failure mode to an observable assertion before selecting a test framework.
Use isolated unit tests for deterministic logic, contract tests for module and provider boundaries, integration tests for real composition, and acceptance tests for business journeys.
Fixtures use explicit tenant and enterprise context, stable business codes, least-privilege identities, and safe cleanup. Never depend on accidental developer data or test only as administrator.
A passing happy path is incomplete until denial, boundary, duplicate, concurrency, timeout, partial failure, recovery, upgrade, and existing-behavior regression are covered.

sections.heading: Evidence and maintenance
items: Record command, version, configuration profile, topology, dependencies, start and end time, result, failures, and artifact location so another team can reproduce the decision.

Separate mocked provider compatibility from qualified live-provider evidence. Local NodeCache success does not prove Redis or Hazelcast behavior, and a monoServer run does not prove distributed ownership.
Flaky tests are defects: classify timing, shared state, order dependence, external instability, and resource leakage, then repair or quarantine with an owner and expiry.
Update tests and beginner documentation in the same implementation change; generated reports supplement but never replace maintained contract explanation.

sections.heading: Release decision
items: Summarize passed, failed, skipped, flaky, and not-applicable cases with risk, owner, and evidence rather than reporting only a total count.
Block release when an authoritative contract, security boundary, data migration, recovery path, or required topology lacks evidence.
Retain reports according to policy and link failures to fixes and regression tests so the next release does not rediscover the same defect.

sections.heading: Required dimensions
items: Positive: the intended authorized workflow succeeds.
Negative: invalid, missing, unauthorized, wrong-principal, and wrong-tenant requests fail safely.
Boundary: empty, maximum, transition, concurrency, timeout, retry, replay, pagination, and size limits.
Contract: schemas, routes, statuses, events, provider interfaces, generated artifacts, and backward compatibility.
Integration: real module boundaries and qualified local providers where feasible; mocks alone are not completion evidence.
Regression: existing capabilities, base modules, custom layers, imports, documentation, and generated context remain valid.

sections.heading: Topology and resilience
items: Use MonoServer for fast local integration while functionality is emerging.
Verify relevant modules independently in modular topology before production readiness; module ownership matters more than a fixed server list.

Test startup ordering, dependency absence, asynchronous registration, stale leases, restart, provider outage, partial failure, retry/backoff, idempotency, recovery, graceful shutdown, and observability.
For staged/online publishing, test separate systems or schemas, approval boundaries, publication, cache invalidation, failure recovery, and online non-versioned behavior.

sections.heading: Security and release evidence
items: Test human login separately from module/service and cron credentials.
Prove tenant/enterprise isolation, least privilege, secrets handling, response masking, audit, abuse controls, and browser protections where applicable.
Run focused tests first, then repository governance and relevant baseline suites; regenerate derived documentation/context before its validators.
Record exact commands, results, limitations, environment assumptions, and untested production dependencies.

sections.heading: Complete guide: How To Test Nodics Changes
paragraphs: Testing in Nodics proves that capabilities still work after framework, project, configuration, or generated-artifact changes.
Tests are not only for finding bugs. They are part of the platform contract.

sections.heading: Beginner Summary
paragraphs: Testing in Nodics answers four questions:

| Question | Example proof |
| --- | --- |
| Does the default framework behavior still work? | Framework/module test passes |
| Does the project override work? | Later-module override test passes |
| Is the behavior secure and tenant-safe? | Permission, auth, tenant, cache, and data isolation tests pass |
| Are generated artifacts still aligned with source? | Generated schema/API/OpenAPI/LLM tests pass |
Do not only test the happy path. A good Nodics change proves success, failure, permission denial, tenant behavior, configuration override, and generated artifact alignment where relevant.

sections.heading: Choose The Right Test
paragraphs: Use broader suites before committing or releasing.

Nodics testing is layered in the same way as the framework. A module can own common tests, environment-specific tests, generated schema/API tests, provider tests, topology tests, and override/customization tests.
The goal is not only to prove one function works. The goal is to prove the capability still works through the hierarchy.

sections.heading: Common Commands
paragraphs:
```bash
npm run test:config
npm run test:tooling
```

sections.heading: What To Test For A New Feature
items: Valid input.
Invalid input.
Permission failure.
Tenant behavior.
Configuration override behavior.
Runtime behavior if runtime configuration is involved.
Generated API behavior if schemas or routes changed.
Documentation and generated context if source files changed.
default framework behavior;
later module override behavior;
configuration override behavior;
tenant-specific behavior when tenant context is involved;
consolidated runtime behavior;
modular process behavior when modules communicate across servers.

sections.heading: Test Selection Guide
paragraphs:
| Change type | Start with | Also consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript syntax or file-level edit | `npm run check:syntax` | `npm run quality:docs` |
| Configuration or module metadata | `npm run test:config` | `npm run test:basic` |
| API route/controller/facade/service | Route contract and focused capability test | `npm run docs:openapi`, `npm run test:basic` |
| Schema or generated CRUD | `npm run test:generated` | `npm run build`, `npm run docs:openapi` |
| Import/export | `npm run test:import` | Capability tests and tenant tests |
| Cache | `npm run test:cache` | Redis release gate only when Redis behavior changed |
| Auth, permission, tenant | Header/auth/security suites | `npm run test:basic` |
| Runtime configuration | `npm run test:runtime-overrides` | Dynamo/runtime governance tests |
| Topology/server/node behavior | `npm run test:topology` | Consolidated and modular topology tests |
| Documentation or AI guidance | `npm run quality:docs`, `npm run llm:validate` | `npm run llm:generate` first |

sections.heading: Live Tests
paragraphs: Some tests require live infrastructure such as Redis.
Live tests are explicit and guarded. They do not silently use shared developer, staging, or production data.

sections.heading: Documentation Checks
paragraphs:
```bash
npm run docs:coverage:source -- --limit=20
npm run docs:coverage:contracts -- --limit=20
```
If a source file changes, make sure file-level documentation and exported method documentation remain complete.

sections.heading: Generated Context
paragraphs: When source behavior or documentation changes, regenerate and validate LLM context:

```bash
npm run llm:generate
npm run llm:validate
```

Generated LLM context is part of the verification story. It helps future AI tools and developers understand which files, tests, extension points, generated artifacts, and documentation belong to a module.

sections.heading: What To Avoid
items: Only running the test that proves your happy path.
Skipping generated tests after schema or route changes.
Running live tests against unsafe data.
Editing generated tests manually as the source of truth.
Updating code without updating documentation.

sections.heading: Beginner Failure Handling
paragraphs: Do not hide a failing test by weakening the assertion unless the product contract intentionally changed and the documentation also explains that change.
items: Read the first failed assertion.
Identify the owner: module, route, schema, service, config, provider, or generated artifact.
Check whether the failure is from source behavior or stale generated output.
Fix the source definition or implementation.
Regenerate generated artifacts when needed.
Rerun the smallest failed test.
Rerun the broader suite only after the focused test is green.
